  result <- paired |> dplyr::filter(.data$population == .env$population,
    .data$model == .env$model, .data$metric == .env$metric)
  stopifnot(nrow(result) == 1)
  sprintf("%.5f (95%% interval %.5f to %.5f)", result$difference, result$lower, result$upper)
}
model_interval <- function(population, model, metric, digits = 3) {
  result <- model_intervals |> dplyr::filter(.data$population == .env$population,
    .data$model == .env$model, .data$metric == .env$metric)
  stopifnot(nrow(result) == 1)
  if (is.na(result$estimate)) return("Not ranked")
  sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f (%.", digits, "f to %.", digits, "f)"),
    result$estimate, result$lower, result$upper)
}

    knitr::kable(align = c("l", rep("r", 5)))
}

## Findings in plain language

More seedlings were a useful clue to later sapling entry, but not a guarantee:
only `r high$conditions_with_new_tally` of `r high$conditions` sampled forest
conditions with more than 20 seedlings initially had a new live maple sapling
recorded at the next visit. Adding measurements of existing maple saplings and
larger maples did not clearly improve prediction. Separately, following tagged
saplings showed that some left the size class by growing, not dying.

Here, a sapling has a trunk at least 1 inch but less than 5 inches in diameter
at breast height. A new recorded sapling is not an individually tracked baseline
seedling. These sample results do not establish statewide regeneration rates,
diagnose why entry was absent, or identify a forest treatment.

[Project overview](../index.qmd) ·
[Study map and figures](spatial-context.qmd) ·
[Code and aggregate evidence](https://github.com/dineshpotla/canopy-to-cohort)
:::

## Abstract

I examined whether ordinary Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) seedling
counts predict recorded sugar-maple (*Acer saccharum*) sapling recruitment
in Michigan northern hardwoods and whether existing maple size structure
improves prediction. The cohort contained `r cohort$conditions` intervals on
`r cohort$physical_plots` physical plots across `r cohort$counties` counties,
with baseline visits in 2011–2018 and follow-ups in 2018–2025;
`r cohort$new_saplings` new live saplings occurred in `r cohort$recruit_conditions`
conditions. I compared four prespecified logistic models using county-level
cross-validation and 300 county-bootstrap resamples per population with model
refitting. After accounting for sampled coverage and elapsed time, count-model
AUC was `r sprintf("%.3f", all_count$roc_auc)` overall and
`r sprintf("%.3f", positive_count$roc_auc)` among 672 conditions with baseline
seedlings. Counts improved Brier score relative to observation design alone,
although the improvement among conditions with seedlings was uncertain. Adding maple sapling
density and established-maple basal area changed Brier score by
`r contrast("All eligible pairs", "Maple stages and design")` overall; the
corresponding interval among conditions with seedlings also crossed zero.
Separately, 1,580 comparable tagged
saplings included 334 recorded deaths, 1,188 live saplings, and 58 live stems
reaching 12.7 cm diameter. Seedling counts were informative about recorded
entry, but the additional value of maple size structure was uncertain.
These retrospective, unweighted comparisons do not establish regeneration
adequacy or justify an operational management rule.

## Study implications

Seedling counts were associated with new sugar-maple saplings recorded at the
next inventory, but abundant seedlings do not establish successful replacement
of canopy trees. In this Michigan sample, adding the
abundance of existing maple saplings and larger maples did not clearly improve
prediction over counts alone. Managers should distinguish recorded sapling
entry from adequate regeneration and retain simple benchmarks when evaluating
more elaborate indicators. The study does not identify a treatment, diagnose
deer damage, or validate a rule for allocating field visits.

## Introduction {#research-context}

Successful regeneration requires seedlings to advance into larger size classes.
Michigan field studies describe plentiful small
seedlings alongside limited larger regeneration [@henry2021]. Sugar-maple age
structure in managed northern hardwoods also shows that small-diameter stems
may be old; existing saplings do not necessarily represent recent establishment
[@henry2023]. These studies differ from standard FIA in their stand samples
and size definitions, so their estimates cannot be treated as statewide
rates for the cohort examined here.

Previous FIA research has examined the relationship between seedling
measurements and subsequent recruitment. Harris and colleagues compared
one seedling class with six height classes using boosted regression trees,
including conspecific sapling abundance and tree basal area as candidate
predictors. Their species-specific analyses were restricted to subplots with
baseline seedlings, and taller seedlings were particularly informative
[@harris2022]. Their work provides a basis for evaluating the contribution
of both seedling measurements and existing conspecific size classes.
Recent northeastern studies distinguish
small-seedling composition from established sapling abundance [@harris2026]
and examine recovery after disturbance over longer intervals
[@harris2026disturbance].

I examine how much information routinely available seedling counts provide
about recorded sapling entry after accounting for sampled coverage and the
time between inventories. I then test whether existing maple saplings and
larger trees improve prediction on the same observations. This regional
comparison complements earlier FIA studies while distinguishing recruitment
from changes in the status of previously tagged saplings. Differences in
subplot populations, seedling definitions, and validation procedures prevent
direct comparison with published AUC values from studies using regeneration
indicator (RI) measurements.

I set three primary objectives: quantify the predictive contribution of ordinary
seedling counts, assess the additional contribution of maple sapling density
and established-maple basal area, and describe the subsequent fates of tagged
baseline saplings. I also evaluated fixed survey-selection strategies and
examined the comparability of ordinary counts with RI length measurements.
These secondary analyses address possible applications and measurement
extensions of the main study.

## Methods

### Source and cohort

I used the pinned Michigan FIADB SQLite snapshot and current-evaluation
cohort, EVALID 262501, rather than all historical intervals. Baseline ecological
eligibility is accessible northern hardwood forest (type group 800) with live
established sugar maple at least five inches diameter. The selected baseline
forest-type codes are 801, 802, 805, and 809. Follow-up forest type need not remain
in group 800. The source pair construction requires an intended plot predecessor,
one-to-one condition mapping, at least 90% mapped-area overlap relative to both
visits, and a 4.5–8.5-year interval. I document the selection and joins in the
[analysis decisions](../docs/analysis-decisions.md#source-and-cohort).

The recruitment audit additionally verifies sampled forest and mapped
microplot-condition area at both visits. Both visits use the national design,
the same offset microplot arrangement, and manual versions at least 5.1.
I treated follow-ups as remeasurements and retained production QA codes 1 and 7.
QA 7 is a supervised production check, not an invalid duplicate
[@burrill2025fiadb].

Direct subplot predecessor identifiers (`PREV_SBP_CN`) are entirely
unpopulated in this snapshot. I reconstructed continuity from the verified
plot predecessor, subplot number, and microplot condition-change matrix.
Nine source pairs failed the conservative matrix-versus-condition proportion
check; one contains unresolved newly recorded saplings. I excluded these ten
pairs rather than assigning zero outcomes. One separately verified sampled
follow-up has no live TREE records and `BALIVE=0`; its missing derived tree
metrics are reconciled to zero only in the new recruitment dataset.

The starting current-evaluation dataset contains 932 condition intervals.
The nine inconsistent mappings and one ambiguous-entry interval are distinct
exclusions, leaving 922. The 914 exact-overlap intervals and the 672 intervals
with baseline seedlings are alternative subsets of that retained cohort,
not additional sequential exclusions. Conditions represent mapped forest
domains within a plot; a physical plot can therefore contribute more than
one condition. The analytical unit is one condition observed across its two
linked visits, not a seedling, individual microplot, or independent stand.

Eligible rows must have complete, finite outcomes and predictor fields.
The modeling code stops on missing required values rather than silently
dropping different rows for different models. I did not impute predictors.
I set absent species tallies to zero only after sampled-forest eligibility and
record checks; I did not assign zero to an unsampled or ambiguous interval.

### Recorded recruitment endpoint

The binary response is at least one new live sugar-maple sapling at follow-up:
`SPCD=318`, `STATUSCD=1`, diameter at least one and less than five inches
(2.54 to less than 12.7 cm), `RECONCILECD=1`, and no predecessor TREE record.
Candidates must occur on a comparable shared sampled microplot. Reconcile code
1 can also describe entry on formerly nonforest land, so it is insufficient
without the preceding sampling-frame checks [@burrill2025fiadb].

These are recorded surviving entrants into the FIA sapling class, not individual
baseline seedlings followed through time. Entrants that die before remeasurement
or exceed the restricted size class are not counted. Large newly recorded
subplot trees are excluded because sampled area increases at the five-inch
boundary. Exact mapped-area overlap is a sensitivity analysis; mapped fractions
do not establish an individual stem's lineage or exact location.

### Predictors and fixed comparisons

I treated all eligible pairs and the subset with baseline seedlings detected as
principal analysis populations and fit models separately. The second population
asks whether measurements distinguish entrants among conditions already
containing seedlings. Both use four fixed logistic models:

1. Training-sample prevalence only.
2. Observation design: baseline microplot coverage and realized interval.
3. Count and design: those variables plus `log1p` ordinary maple seedling count.
4. Stages and design: the count model plus `log1p` baseline maple sapling
   density and `log1p` established-maple basal area.

Ordinary counts sum `SEEDLING.TREECOUNT` and are checked against
`TREECOUNT_CALC`. Sapling density uses FIA stem expansion and sampled microplot
area; established-maple basal area uses live stems at least five inches diameter
and the corresponding sampled area. Coverage is a model covariate, not a
claim that raw counts were collected over identical footprints. Standard
hardwood tallies omit the smallest seedlings, and counts above five may be
estimated [@fiafield2023]. A recorded count is not necessarily an exact number
of independent seed-origin individuals.

Training-only standardization precedes fitting. The objective is summed binomial
negative log likelihood plus $\lambda\sum_j\beta_j^2/2$ for slopes, with
$\lambda=1$ and an unpenalized intercept. This fixed ridge penalty was not tuned
to optimize the findings. Ordinary GLM coefficient p-values are not attached
to penalized fits. No additional competitor, beech, climate, or treatment
predictor is selected after examining these recruitment results.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-recruitment-predictors
#| tbl-cap: "Predictor definitions and transformations. All quantities except the realized interval are measured at baseline. Log transformations use the listed source units."
tibble::tribble(
  ~Predictor, ~`Source quantity and unit`, ~Transformation, ~`First included`,
  "Microplot coverage", "MICRPROP_UNADJ; fraction of nominal microplot area in the condition", "Identity", "Design",
  "Elapsed interval", "Time between linked measurements; years", "Identity", "Design",
  "Maple seedling count", "Sum of TREECOUNT across sampled condition microplots; count", "log(1 + count)", "Count",
  "Maple sapling density", "Sum of sapling TPA_UNADJ divided by MICRPROP_UNADJ; stems per acre", "log(1 + density)", "Stages",
  "Established maple basal area", "Expanded live-maple basal area for diameter at least 5 inches; square feet per acre", "log(1 + basal area)", "Stages"
) |> knitr::kable(align = c("l", "l", "l", "l"))
```

I transformed each predictor before centering and dividing by its training-sample
standard deviation. I applied the same training center and scale to held-out
observations. I used a scale of one for a constant training predictor to prevent
division by zero. The model is
$p_i=1/(1+\exp(-\eta_i))$, where
$\eta_i=\beta_0+\sum_j\beta_j z_{ij}$ and the included standardized predictors
follow the four-model sequence. Coverage and interval enter as estimated
slopes, not offsets. The response is binary entry, so the model does not
estimate the number of new saplings or an annual recruitment rate.

The production optimizer uses Newton steps with a backtracking line search,
a maximum of 100 iterations, and finite-coefficient and gradient checks.
Model dimensions are zero, two, three, and five slopes, respectively, plus
the intercept. Coefficients from subsequent fits to each complete analysis
population are descriptive summaries; all performance claims use held-out
predictions, not those full-population fitted values. The appendix reports
the coefficients without unpenalized standard errors or significance stars.

### Validation and uncertainty

Five folds hold out entire counties, balancing condition counts without using
outcomes in assignment. All models within a population use identical
observations and folds. Every physical plot stays in one fold. Scaling and
fitting use training counties only. County separation prevents the same county
from entering both sets, but does not impose a distance buffer between nearby
plots in neighboring counties or guarantee environmental separation.

Brier score and log loss evaluate probabilities; AUC and average precision
(AP) evaluate discrimination. Losses average equally over condition intervals:
they are neither plot-balanced nor FIA survey-weighted population estimates.
I estimated calibration intercept and slope jointly by regressing outcomes
on held-out log odds. These are diagnostics, not recalibration of predictions;
the joint intercept is not a separately fitted calibration-in-the-large
intercept. Mean predicted probability and the observed-to-expected ratio
are also exported. Rank metrics for the prevalence benchmark are omitted
because differences in fold-specific prevalence do not constitute a meaningful
individual ranking.

Specifically, the Brier score is the mean squared probability error,
$n^{-1}\sum_i(y_i-p_i)^2$. Log loss is
$-n^{-1}\sum_i[y_i\log(p_i)+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)]$; probabilities are bounded
between $10^{-12}$ and $1-10^{-12}$ for numerical scoring. Lower losses are
better. AUC compares event and nonevent rankings with half credit for tied
probabilities. AP sums precision over increments in recall after grouping
equal probabilities. AP depends on event prevalence, so the two nested
populations are not interchangeable benchmarks. I report probability loss,
ranking, and calibration separately because improvement in one need not
imply improvement in the others.

I ordered counties by descending condition count, used county identifier to
break ties, and assigned each county to the currently least-loaded fold. Fold
size, then county count, then fold number resolve assignment ties. This is a single
deterministic partition, not repeated random cross-validation. The two
populations receive their own size-balanced partition. Metrics pool all
out-of-fold predictions within each population rather than averaging its
five fold-specific AUC values. Appendix fold denominators show how many
events actually support each held-out comparison.

I used `r bootstrap$resamples_requested[[1]]` resamples per population of whole
counties, repeating scaling and all held-out fits.
All `r sum(bootstrap$resamples_succeeded)` resamples succeed. Original fold
assignments, model set, and penalty remain fixed. Paired differences subtract
the reference model on identical cases; negative Brier differences favor the
added information. Percentile intervals characterize this resampling scheme.
They exclude uncertainty from selecting the question, cohort, model set,
and source snapshot. These data were already explored; this is not
preregistration or external validation. The 300 draws provide finite Monte
Carlo precision for the interval endpoints; their displayed digits should not
be read as equally precise inferential information. No equivalence margin or
minimum useful improvement was specified, and no multiple-comparison correction
is applied. Interpretation emphasizes the matched Brier contrasts; additional
metrics and secondary analyses are descriptive.

Each bootstrap draw samples the population's counties with replacement,
using the same number of county draws as observed counties. Every condition
in a selected county receives its county's sampling multiplicity as a
frequency weight. All copies remain in that county's original fold, so
resampling cannot put a duplicate county into both training and testing.
Weighted training means, sample standard deviations, model fits, and pooled
scores are recomputed in each draw. Counties drawn zero times have no
evaluation weight. The reported limits are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles
of the 300 resulting metrics or paired differences, not standard errors
calculated by treating 922 conditions as independent replicates. The stored
seed is 20260908 in each population; this does not make the nested analyses
independent.

Descriptive count-bin intervals use a separate 2,000-draw county resampling
of observed event fractions, without fitting a model. A bin with no observed
events has a degenerate empirical interval at zero; it does not establish a
zero population risk. These intervals and the model-refit intervals answer
different questions and should not be combined.

Fixed sensitivities restrict to exact overlap or follow-up manual version at
least 9, or use penalties 0 and 4. A retrospective temporal assessment trains
on follow-ups before 2023 and tests 2023 onward, with no shared physical plots.
Realized interval is known at follow-up. Accordingly, these are conditional
next-visit assessments, not validated fixed-horizon forecasts available at
baseline. Count agreement and manual-version screening do not establish that
every historical field procedure is identical; individual baseline regional
editions were not all verified.

### Linked sapling fates

A companion cohort follows live tagged baseline maple saplings on the expected
successor plot before restricting follow-up species, status, or diameter.
Comparable recorded death, live persistence below five inches, and live
advancement to at least five inches are separated from frame inconsistency,
species reidentification, and no-longer-sampled records. I assessed fate
eligibility separately from the new-entrant outcome: an ambiguous new arrival
does not alone invalidate an existing tagged stem's link. I calculated annual
diameter difference as follow-up minus baseline diameter divided by elapsed
years and summarized it only for comparable surviving maples. No mortality mechanism,
treatment effect, or independent-stem sampling assumption is imposed.

### Use of AI assistance

I used OpenAI Codex to assist with literature searching, analysis-code
development and checking, and manuscript revision. Computational checks do not
constitute independent scientific review. I retain responsibility for the data
interpretation, references, and submitted content.

## Results

### Cohort support

The final cohort contains `r cohort$conditions` condition intervals on
`r cohort$physical_plots` physical plots in `r cohort$counties` counties.
There are `r cohort$new_saplings` qualifying saplings in
`r cohort$recruit_conditions` conditions. Baseline measurements span
`r calendar$baseline_year_min`–`r calendar$baseline_year_max`; follow-ups span
`r calendar$followup_year_min`–`r calendar$followup_year_max`. Observed intervals
range from `r sprintf("%.2f", calendar$interval_years_min)` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", calendar$interval_years_max)` years, with median
`r sprintf("%.1f", calendar$interval_years_median)`. Baseline microplot coverage
ranges from `r percent(calendar$coverage_min)` to `r percent(calendar$coverage_max)`,
with median `r percent(calendar$coverage_median)`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-recruitment-flow
#| tbl-cap: "Analysis support. The baseline-detected subset is nested within all eligible pairs; these are unweighted sample counts."
support |> dplyr::transmute(Population = short_population(.data$population),
  Conditions = .data$conditions, Plots = .data$physical_plots, Counties = .data$counties,
  `With entry` = .data$events, `New saplings` = .data$new_saplings) |> knitr::kable()
```

All 100 recruit-bearing conditions had seedlings at baseline. The 250 eligible
baseline-zero conditions had no qualifying entry, which does not establish a
true probability of zero. Exact overlap retains 914 intervals and all 169
entrants; the eight excluded nonexact intervals have no qualifying entrants.
The full [cohort flow](../outputs/tables/recruitment-cohort-flow.csv) preserves
source counts and alternative restrictions without presenting them as successive
exclusions.

### Seedling abundance and observed entry

```{r}
#| label: fig-recruitment-counts
#| fig-cap: "Recorded new-sapling entry by baseline seedling count. Error bars resample whole counties; descriptive bins are not stocking thresholds."
#| fig-alt: "Entry frequency rises with baseline seedling count, reaching approximately 26 percent among conditions with more than twenty recorded seedlings."
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("outputs", "figures", "10_recruitment_counts.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-recruitment-counts
#| tbl-cap: "Numerators and denominators for the abundance comparison."
count_intervals |> dplyr::transmute(`Baseline count` = .data$count_group, Conditions = .data$conditions,
  `With new tally` = .data$conditions_with_new_tally,
  `Recorded entry` = percent(.data$recruitment_fraction),
  `95% interval` = paste(percent(.data$lower), "to", percent(.data$upper))) |> knitr::kable()
```

Recorded entry rises from one of 82 conditions with one seedling to
`r high$conditions_with_new_tally` of `r high$conditions`
(`r percent(high$recruitment_fraction)`) with more than twenty. The remaining
`r high$conditions - high$conditions_with_new_tally` high-count conditions have
no qualifying new tally. These are observations on the sampled footprint, not
stand-level failure rates. Neither the 20-count boundary nor one new sapling
is an ecological adequacy threshold.

Existing maple saplings also show a descriptive association: 86 of 567 conditions
with baseline saplings record entry, compared with 14 of 355 without saplings.
This unadjusted contrast does not measure their incremental predictive value.

### Held out performance

```{r}
#| label: tbl-recruitment-cv-all
#| tbl-cap: "County-held-out performance across all 922 eligible intervals. Lower Brier and log loss are better; AP denotes average precision."
model_table("All eligible pairs")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-recruitment-cv-positive
#| tbl-cap: "County-held-out performance among 672 baseline seedling detections, with separately fitted models."
model_table("Baseline seedlings detected")
```

The count model's AUC is `r sprintf("%.3f", all_count$roc_auc)` overall and
`r sprintf("%.3f", positive_count$roc_auc)` among baseline detections.
Adding maple stages yields `r sprintf("%.3f", all_stage$roc_auc)` and
`r sprintf("%.3f", positive_stage$roc_auc)`, respectively. The lower conditional
discrimination illustrates the harder task of distinguishing entry within
already seedling-bearing conditions. Pooled ranking partly benefits from
separating baseline zeros from positive counts.

Count-model mean predicted probabilities are
`r percent(all_count$mean_predicted_probability)` overall and
`r percent(positive_count$mean_predicted_probability)` among baseline detections;
observed fractions are `r percent(all_count$event_fraction)` and
`r percent(positive_count$event_fraction)`. Corresponding observed-to-expected
ratios are `r sprintf("%.3f", all_count$observed_expected_ratio)` and
`r sprintf("%.3f", positive_count$observed_expected_ratio)`.
Calibration slopes below one, especially within baseline detections, caution
against interpreting near-matching average probabilities as established local
calibration or transportability. I retain complete calibration diagnostics in
the [validation table](../outputs/tables/recruitment-model-validation.csv).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-recruitment-calibration
#| tbl-cap: "Calibration of pooled county-held-out predictions. All denotes all 922 eligible intervals; Detected denotes the 672 baseline-detected intervals. O/E is observed events divided by summed predicted probabilities."
cv |> dplyr::filter(.data$model != "Prevalence") |>
  dplyr::transmute(Population = population_code(.data$population), Model = short_model(.data$model),
    `Mean predicted` = percent(.data$mean_predicted_probability),
    `Joint intercept` = sprintf("%.3f", .data$calibration_intercept),
    Slope = sprintf("%.3f", .data$calibration_slope),
    `O/E` = sprintf("%.3f", .data$observed_expected_ratio)) |> knitr::kable()
```

The count-model calibration slope is
`r sprintf("%.3f", all_count$calibration_slope)` overall and
`r sprintf("%.3f", positive_count$calibration_slope)` within detections;
the stage-model slopes are `r sprintf("%.3f", all_stage$calibration_slope)`
and `r sprintf("%.3f", positive_stage$calibration_slope)`. These point
diagnostics suggest overly dispersed log-odds predictions, especially in
the detected subset, but I did not estimate calibration-parameter uncertainty
intervals. Near-unit O/E describes average agreement and does not
resolve probability errors within subgroups. Absolute Brier and AUC
intervals are reported in the appendix; model comparisons use paired
differences rather than overlap of separate marginal intervals.

### Incremental information and matched capacity

```{r}
#| label: fig-recruitment-added-value
#| fig-cap: "Paired Brier differences on matched observations, with full-refit county-bootstrap 95% intervals. Negative differences favor the added information."
#| fig-alt: "Counts improve pooled Brier beyond observation design; added maple stages have small point improvements with intervals spanning zero in both populations."
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("outputs", "figures", "11_recruitment_incremental_value.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-recruitment-differences
#| tbl-cap: "Named model minus reference Brier differences. Intervals are percentile summaries, not equivalence tests."
paired |> dplyr::filter(.data$metric == "brier_score") |>
  dplyr::transmute(Population = short_population(.data$population),
    Addition = ifelse(.data$model == "Seedling count and design", "Count to design", "Stages to count"),
    Difference = sprintf("%.5f", .data$difference),
    `95% interval` = sprintf("%.5f to %.5f", .data$lower, .data$upper)) |> knitr::kable()
```

Count addition improves pooled Brier by
`r contrast("All eligible pairs", "Seedling count and design")`.
Within baseline detections the difference is
`r contrast("Baseline seedlings detected", "Seedling count and design")`;
its interval crosses zero despite improved ranking. Stage additions produce
small point improvements in both populations, with intervals spanning benefit
and harm. This does not establish equivalence or demonstrate that stage
information could never be useful.

The probability scores do not give identical strength of evidence. Among
baseline detections, count addition changes log loss by
`r contrast("Baseline seedlings detected", "Seedling count and design", "log_loss")`,
whose interval excludes zero even though the Brier interval crosses zero.
Its AUC and AP contrasts also favor counts in the stored resampling results.
Counts therefore improve ranking and log loss in that subset, while their
average squared-error improvement is less certain. The metrics describe
different aspects of predictive performance.

For stage addition, the AUC differences are
`r contrast("All eligible pairs", "Maple stages and design", "roc_auc")`
overall and
`r contrast("Baseline seedlings detected", "Maple stages and design", "roc_auc")`
within detections. Stage-addition intervals for log loss and AP also cross
zero. Thus, the higher stage-model point AUC does not establish a reliable
increment over the count model. The appendix includes all matched log-loss,
AUC, and AP contrasts, including results that qualify the headline finding.

At the same highest-probability 25% capacity, the count model captures 60
recruit-bearing conditions among 230 selected overall; the stage model captures
58. Among baseline detections, the respective numbers are 44 and 43 among 168.
Selection uses held-out probabilities and stable source-key tie breaking;
tie-neutral results are also exported. This capacity is diagnostic, not a
recommended survey rule or a measured fieldwork budget.

### Sensitivities and temporal assessment

Exact overlap, the declared penalty alternatives, and the recent-manual
restriction do not reverse the broad discrimination pattern. The recent-manual
restriction changes both the sample and calendar distribution; it is not an
isolated experiment on protocol effects. The
[complete sensitivity table](../outputs/tables/recruitment-model-sensitivities.csv)
reports every fitted benchmark, denominator, and metric.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-recruitment-sensitivity-detail
#| tbl-cap: "Fixed sensitivity comparisons on matched cases. Each Brier pair lists count then stage; the difference is stage minus count. No new uncertainty intervals were computed for these sensitivities."
count_sensitivity <- sensitivity |> dplyr::filter(.data$model == "Seedling count and design")
stage_sensitivity <- sensitivity |> dplyr::filter(.data$model == "Maple stages and design")
matched_sensitivity <- dplyr::inner_join(count_sensitivity, stage_sensitivity,
  by = c("population", "sensitivity", "observations", "events"), suffix = c("_count", "_stage"))
stopifnot(nrow(matched_sensitivity) == 8L)
matched_sensitivity |> dplyr::transmute(Population = population_code(.data$population),
  Restriction = dplyr::recode(.data$sensitivity, "Exact mapped overlap" = "Exact overlap",
    "Follow-up manual >=9" = "Manual at least 9", "Ridge lambda 4" = "Penalty 4", "Unpenalized" = "Penalty 0"),
  `N / events` = paste(.data$observations, .data$events, sep = " / "),
  `Brier count / stage` = sprintf("%.5f / %.5f", .data$brier_score_count, .data$brier_score_stage),
  Difference = sprintf("%.5f", .data$brier_score_stage - .data$brier_score_count),
  `AUC count / stage` = sprintf("%.3f / %.3f", .data$roc_auc_count, .data$roc_auc_stage)) |> knitr::kable()
```

The recent-manual restriction retains 787 intervals with 92 events overall
and 573 with 92 events among baseline detections. Exact-overlap support is
914 and 668 intervals, respectively, with all 100 events retained in each.
The alternative penalties keep the original denominators. Stage-minus-count
Brier differences remain negative at their point estimates, but this sign
stability is not a new test of improvement. These analyses retain the
original county assignments within each population and do not search for
a more favorable fold partition.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-recruitment-temporal
#| tbl-cap: "Retrospective later-year performance. Follow-ups before 2023 train the models; 2023 onward test them."
temporal |> dplyr::transmute(Population = short_population(.data$population), Model = short_model(.data$model),
    `Test N` = .data$observations, Events = .data$events,
    Brier = sprintf("%.5f", .data$brier_score),
    AUC = ifelse(is.na(.data$roc_auc), "Not ranked", sprintf("%.3f", .data$roc_auc))) |> knitr::kable()
```

Training contains 547 intervals and 59 event-bearing conditions overall;
testing contains 375 intervals and 41 event-bearing conditions. The
baseline-detected counterparts contain 397 and 275 intervals, with the same
event counts. No physical plot crosses the split. Stage-model test AUC is
approximately 0.807 overall and 0.721 within baseline detections.
This single retrospective split has no paired bootstrap uncertainty assessment
and does not establish future-inventory or out-of-state performance. The
[split support table](../outputs/tables/recruitment-model-temporal-support.csv)
reports the changing calendar, manual, interval, plot, and county distributions.

Overall, training comprises 535 plots in 55 counties and testing comprises
368 plots in 49 counties. The detected subset comprises 395 training plots
in 41 counties and 272 test plots in 36 counties. Median duration is seven
years in all four groups. Follow-up manuals range from 8 to 9 in training
and from 9 to 9.4 in testing; all test intervals use manual 9 or later.
The split therefore evaluates both calendar change and changes in sample
composition. Counties can recur across years even though physical plots do
not, distinguishing this assessment from the county-held-out analysis.

### Linked sapling fates

Of 1,593 live tagged baseline maple saplings, 1,580 have comparable biological
fates. Nine stems fail frame consistency, three living stems are reidentified
as red maple, and one is no longer sampled under a cruiser-error reconciliation.
These 13 remain in the accounting but are not assigned biological outcomes.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-recruitment-fates
#| tbl-cap: "Tagged baseline saplings with comparable biological fates. Thirteen additional source stems are excluded for the reasons described in the text."
fates |> dplyr::filter(.data$fate_eligible) |>
  dplyr::group_by(.data$fate) |>
  dplyr::summarise(Stems = sum(.data$trees), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::mutate(`Share of comparable stems` = percent(.data$Stems / sum(.data$Stems))) |>
  dplyr::rename(`Recorded state` = .data$fate) |> knitr::kable()
```

The 58 larger live stems advanced out of the sapling size class rather than
died. Among the 1,246 comparable surviving maples, median annual diameter
difference is `r sprintf("%.4f", growth$median_increment_inches_year)` inches
per year. There are `r growth$zero_increment` zero and
`r growth$negative_increment` negative differences. Rounding,
measurement-point changes, and survivor selection limit interpretation.
These observations cannot establish suppression, cohort age, or future
canopy replacement; individual stem numbers are not independent sample sizes.

The 10th and 90th percentiles of annual diameter difference are
`r sprintf("%.4f", growth$p10)` and `r sprintf("%.4f", growth$p90)` inches
per year. Zero differences represent `r percent(growth$zero_increment / growth$survivors)`
of comparable survivors and negative differences represent
`r percent(growth$negative_increment / growth$survivors)`. These are
unweighted stem summaries over variable intervals, not fitted growth curves
or county-adjusted mortality estimates. I did not estimate uncertainty intervals
for fate proportions or fit a predictor-based mortality model.

### Secondary survey priority comparison {#survey-priority-comparison}

A separate retrospective diagnostic asks whether model rankings concentrate
conditions with baseline seedlings but no recorded entry. This outcome occurs
in 572 of 672 conditions; it is not independently established survey need.
At a fixed 168-condition capacity, expected no-entry capture is 143 under
random selection, 162 under low raw count, 160 under the count model, and 163
under the stage model. Cutoff ties are integrated rather than favorably ordered.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-recruitment-survey-detail
#| tbl-cap: "All six fixed no-entry selection strategies among 672 baseline detections at a capacity of 168 conditions. Expected targets integrate cutoff ties; the interval describes the selected target fraction, not a paired strategy difference."
survey_primary |> dplyr::transmute(Strategy = .data$policy,
  `Expected targets` = sprintf("%.2f", .data$expected_targets),
  `Selected target fraction` = percent(.data$selected_target_fraction),
  `95% interval` = paste(percent(.data$lower), "to", percent(.data$upper)),
  `All targets captured` = percent(.data$target_capture_fraction)) |> knitr::kable()
```

For the no-entry target, raw counts and predicted entry probabilities are
ranked from low to high. Coverage-normalized count and absence of baseline
saplings provide two additional simple comparators. Expected yield includes
every condition strictly beyond the selection cutoff and assigns the
remaining places uniformly within the cutoff tie. Fractional expected
targets therefore express tie averaging, not fractional observed conditions.
For each strategy, selected target fraction divides expected targets by
168; target capture divides by all 572 no-entry conditions. These answer
different questions. Random selection has a high expected yield because
85.1% of the eligible detected subset already meets this descriptive target.

The stage-minus-raw-count difference in selected target fraction is +0.60
percentage points, with a 95% full-refit county-bootstrap interval of −3.66
to +2.28. A separate 300 resamples per population all succeed. In later-year
testing, raw counts yield 65.18 expected targets among 68 selected, versus 65
for either model. The one-condition point gain is not a demonstrated decision
advantage. Raw-count selection covers 168 plots versus 167 for the stage model,
so equal condition capacity is not equal field cost.

The opposite target of locating entrants yields 41 for high raw counts, 44 for
the count model, and 43 for the stage model among 168 selected baseline
detections. Fixed 10% and 50% capacities likewise do not establish stage-model
dominance. A common seven-year scoring sensitivity changes predictions but not
the observed variable-duration outcomes, so it cannot validate seven-year
probabilities. I retain full [strategy results](../outputs/tables/recruitment-survey-summary.csv),
[paired uncertainty](../outputs/tables/recruitment-survey-paired-differences.csv),
[temporal selection](../outputs/tables/recruitment-survey-temporal.csv), and
[common-horizon comparisons](../outputs/tables/recruitment-survey-common-horizon.csv).
Meaningful net benefit requires defensible consequences of errors
[@vickers2006]; no forest-survey utility threshold is assumed here.

### Secondary length measurement audit

The [RI measurement audit](ri-audit.qmd) retains 90 baseline intervals with
14 recruit-bearing conditions. Ordinary counts equal RI classes at least one
foot long on all 311 matched microplot-condition intervals. Thus, length
distribution—not the collapsed RI total—is the potential extra measurement.
Thirteen events occur among 44 conditions with baseline seedlings at least
five feet long, versus one among 46 without them. This is an unadjusted
descriptive contrast, not a paired held-out improvement over counts.

Only ten development events and four later-year events are available. No height
model is fitted. Annual 2016–2018 supplements were inspected, including an
archived 2016 draft; individual 2012–2015 supplements remain an access gap.
These qualifications constrain the secondary RI finding, not completion of
the ordinary-count and linked-fate analyses.

## Discussion

Ordinary seedling counts contain information about recorded sapling entry in
this selected Michigan sample. The count gradient and pooled probability-loss
improvement argue against dismissing standard tallies as uninformative.
However, discrimination is weaker within baseline detections, and its paired
Brier improvement is uncertain. Abundant seedlings therefore indicate a higher
chance of observing entry without establishing a secure advancing cohort.

The added maple-stage predictors produce only small, uncertain improvements
over a strong count benchmark. They do not improve captured entrants at the
tested equal capacity, and their survey-priority point gain over raw counts
is not reproduced in the later-year comparison. These are substantive limits
of the tested predictors and models, not reasons to continue adding variables
until a preferred explanation appears. Uncertainty spanning zero is not proof
of no effect, practical equivalence, or irrelevance under every model form.

In particular, existing sapling density and larger-tree basal area do not
measure the height distribution of seedlings approaching the sapling boundary.
Their uncertain incremental value therefore does not contradict evidence for
height-resolved inventories [@harris2022]. The additive, transformed linear
predictors also leave nonlinear responses and interactions untested. The
results limit the specific benchmark models evaluated here, not all possible
uses of stage structure.

The fate analysis explains why size-class absence and mortality must remain
distinct. Surviving stems can move beyond the sapling boundary, while species
reidentification and sampling corrections also alter apparent stage membership.
Conversely, a new live sapling at one revisit does not measure all arrivals
during the interval, adequate stocking, genetic origin, or subsequent survival
to the canopy. Neither record-based endpoint supports a causal claim about
browsing, competitors, or management.

### Scope and limitations

The target is retained sampled conditions, not all Michigan forests. Baseline
ecological selection, current-evaluation membership, accessible forest,
remeasurement, comparable area, and unambiguous records restrict inclusion.
The exclusion audit protects outcome interpretation but does not remove
selection bias. County grouping addresses part of the dependence structure;
it does not provide survey weights or independent experimental replication.
The main scores give each condition interval equal weight, so plots contributing
more than one condition receive more total evaluation weight.

Finite event support, estimated seedling tallies, varying sampled area and
exposure duration, model-form choices, incomplete historical manual review,
and one fixed source snapshot limit generalization. Resampling does
not correct all of these limitations. Near-matching mean predicted and observed
event fractions is not evidence of calibration everywhere, and the retrospective
temporal split is not an untouched external test.

The two analysis populations are nested and do not provide independent
replications. Observed entry combines growth into the defined diameter class,
survival until remeasurement, and recording on a small sampled footprint.
Zero recorded entry cannot distinguish slow growth from mortality or absence
of suitable seedlings. Likewise, the tagged-stem fate sample does not follow
the untagged baseline seedlings; it cannot decompose their failure to enter
the sapling class. Unmeasured browsing, understory competition, and disturbance
may influence these processes, but this analysis does not estimate their effects.

### Implications and optional future work

The practical implication is to retain simple count-based benchmarks and state
precisely what they predict. A management tool would additionally require a
defined action, independently assessed survey need or treatment response,
consequences of errors, and relevant external evaluation. No operational
ranking or intervention rule is released.

Length structure is a plausible follow-on hypothesis motivated by earlier FIA
work [@harris2022], not the unfulfilled central objective of this paper.
A [separate design](length-study.qmd) specifies a matched count-versus-length
comparison and evaluation safeguards. Regional inventory acquisition and
field validation are deferred extensions. Wisconsin or Minnesota data are not
required to complete the bounded Michigan results, and no regional outcome or
height-model result is claimed.

## Conclusion

Standard FIA seedling counts provide limited information about next-visit
recorded sugar-maple sapling entry in selected Michigan northern hardwood
conditions. Existing maple sapling density and established-maple basal area
show no clear incremental improvement over the count benchmark under the
specified comparisons. Linked tagged-stem accounting separately identifies
recorded death, persistent live saplings, and surviving advancement beyond the
sapling class. The core finding is an evidence-based boundary on what these
common observations establish—not a claim of regeneration adequacy, biological
failure, or validated management usefulness.

## Reproducibility and evidence

### Data and code availability

The underlying public inventory is distributed through the USDA Forest Service
FIA DataMart [@usfs_datamart]. The analysis uses Michigan evaluation 262501
and the source archive identified by SHA-256
`2c1eb908a47436d4edd0f3ba9e3d647b79a4f36cef972c5ba83277300817aee1`.
The state download URL is updated over time; the evaluation identifier alone
does not fix every source record. Reproducing the reported results therefore
requires the identified snapshot, not an unchecked current download.

Analysis scripts, configuration, an R dependency lockfile, aggregate tables,
and figure data are publicly available in the
[project repository](https://github.com/dineshpotla/canopy-to-cohort).
Record-level derived
datasets and predictions remain local. Exact FIA plot locations are neither
used nor inferred. A version-specific public archive for the recruitment
analysis has not yet been assigned. Cite the exact Git commit when referring
to these results.

### Computational workflow

I maintain the manuscript, endpoint definitions, analysis contracts, aggregate
tables, figures, and tests together. With the pinned source and linked cohort
already built, run:

```bash
make recruitment-core
make test
make submission-audit
make report
```

The core target rebuilds the endpoint, fixed models, figures, survey diagnostic,
RI audits, and manuscript reconciliation. It does not download another state
or fit a length model. `make paper-audit` independently recomputes manuscript
metrics from stored held-out predictions and checks the exported evidence.

Aggregate [paper support](../outputs/tables/recruitment-paper-support.csv),
[numerical checks](../outputs/audits/recruitment-paper-checks.csv),
[paired model differences](../outputs/tables/recruitment-model-paired-differences.csv),
[fate accounting](../outputs/audits/recruitment-sapling-fates.csv), and
[figure data](../outputs/tables/recruitment-model-count-strata-intervals.csv)
accompany the manuscript. Raw inventories, record-level derived data, and
predictions remain local and excluded from version control.
The [analysis decisions](../docs/analysis-decisions.md) record source access
and interpretation limits. Numerical cross-checks assess computational
consistency; they do not replace scientific review or establish external
validity.

## Analytical appendix

### County fold support and fitting diagnostics

The appendix expands the same fixed analysis reported in the main text.
All denotes the 922 eligible intervals and Detected denotes the 672 intervals
with baseline seedlings. An event is a condition with at least one qualifying
new sapling, not the number of saplings. The population-specific partitions
and all model comparisons were fixed before the recruitment fits; the source
snapshot is fixed as described in Methods.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-recruitment-fold-support
#| tbl-cap: "Training and held-out support for each county fold. Every model within a population uses these same rows and outcomes."
fold_diagnostics |> dplyr::filter(.data$model == "Seedling count and design") |>
  dplyr::transmute(Population = population_code(.data$population), Fold = .data$fold,
    `Train N / events` = paste(.data$training_n, .data$training_events, sep = " / "),
    `Test N / events` = paste(.data$test_n, .data$test_events, sep = " / "),
    `Test counties` = .data$test_counties) |> knitr::kable()
```

All `r nrow(fold_diagnostics)` original county-held-out model fits converged.
The largest final absolute gradient component was
`r sprintf("%.2e", max(fold_diagnostics$max_gradient))`, and the largest
absolute coefficient was
`r sprintf("%.3f", max(fold_diagnostics$max_absolute_coefficient))`.
All 300 county-refit bootstrap draws in each population succeeded.
Convergence establishes numerical completion of the specified objective;
it does not establish an adequate sample size, a correct ecological model,
or independent observations. The second numerical implementation described
in the reproducibility handoff checks 40 county-held-out and eight temporal
point-prediction fits, but does not replay the bootstrap intervals.

### Absolute performance uncertainty

```{r}
#| label: tbl-recruitment-absolute-intervals
#| tbl-cap: "Absolute held-out performance with 95% full-refit county-bootstrap intervals. Separate intervals describe each model, not the uncertainty of its difference from another model."
cv |> dplyr::transmute(Population = population_code(.data$population),
  Model = short_model(.data$model),
  `Brier estimate and interval` = mapply(model_interval, .data$population, .data$model,
    MoreArgs = list(metric = "brier_score", digits = 5)),
  `AUC estimate and interval` = mapply(model_interval, .data$population, .data$model,
    MoreArgs = list(metric = "roc_auc", digits = 3))) |> knitr::kable()
```

The wide within-detection AUC intervals reflect uncertainty in separating
100 event conditions from 572 nonevent conditions under county resampling.
No rank score is assigned to the fold-specific prevalence benchmark.
These intervals retain fixed model choices, penalty, and county partition;
they are not repeated-study coverage guarantees across new inventories.

### Paired ranking and log loss contrasts

```{r}
#| label: tbl-recruitment-extended-contrasts
#| tbl-cap: "Additional paired contrasts from the same 300 full-refit county draws per population. Negative log loss and positive AUC or AP differences favor the added information."
paired |> dplyr::filter(.data$metric %in% c("log_loss", "roc_auc", "average_precision")) |>
  dplyr::arrange(.data$population, .data$model, .data$metric) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Population = population_code(.data$population),
    Addition = ifelse(.data$model == "Seedling count and design", "Count to design", "Stages to count"),
    Metric = dplyr::recode(.data$metric, "log_loss" = "Log loss", "roc_auc" = "AUC", "average_precision" = "AP"),
    Difference = sprintf("%.4f", .data$difference),
    `95% interval` = sprintf("%.4f to %.4f", .data$lower, .data$upper)) |> knitr::kable()
```

These are correlated comparisons on the same outcomes. They supplement the
emphasis on Brier contrasts and have not been corrected for multiplicity.
Differences are paired within each bootstrap draw; subtracting limits from
the preceding absolute-interval table would not reproduce them.

### Full population penalized coefficients

```{r}
#| label: tbl-recruitment-coefficients
#| tbl-cap: "Full-population ridge coefficients on the standardized log-odds scale. Each column uses its own population's centers and scales. These are descriptive coefficients, not held-out effect estimates."
coefficients |> dplyr::select(.data$model, .data$term, .data$population,
    .data$penalized_log_odds_coefficient) |>
  dplyr::mutate(population = population_code(.data$population)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = "population", values_from = "penalized_log_odds_coefficient") |>
  dplyr::transmute(Model = short_model(.data$model),
    Term = dplyr::recode(.data$term, "(Intercept)" = "Intercept",
      "z_coverage" = "Coverage", "z_interval" = "Interval",
      "z_seedling_count" = "Log seedling count", "z_sapling_tpa" = "Log sapling density",
      "z_established_ba" = "Log established basal area"),
    All = sprintf("%.4f", .data$All), Detected = sprintf("%.4f", .data$Detected)) |> knitr::kable()
```

A slope describes the fitted log-odds change per one population-specific
standard deviation of the listed transformed predictor, with other terms
held fixed. It is not a per-seedling effect or a causal response to changing
the forest. Intercepts correspond to the population's centered predictors.
Centers and scales for these descriptive fits remain in the saved model
bundle; county-held-out fits use their own training-only scaling instead.

The positive seedling-count and sapling-density slopes and the near-zero
established-basal-area slopes describe these fitted models. They do not
provide coefficient uncertainty, tests of biological importance, or a
variable-importance ranking that accounts for correlated predictors.
The predictive claim depends on held-out model contrasts, not on whether
an individual fitted coefficient is positive or near zero.

### Joint count and sapling strata

```{r}
#| label: tbl-recruitment-joint-strata
#| tbl-cap: "Unadjusted joint distribution of baseline counts, existing saplings, and recorded entry in all eligible intervals. Cells are descriptive, not randomized or matched comparisons."
joint_strata |> dplyr::transmute(`Baseline count` = .data$count_group,
  `Existing saplings` = ifelse(.data$saplings_present, "Present", "Absent"),
  Conditions = .data$conditions, `With entry` = .data$conditions_with_new_tally,
  `Entry fraction` = percent(.data$recruitment_fraction)) |> knitr::kable()
```

In the greater-than-20 count bin, entry occurs in 59 of 202 conditions with
existing saplings and 13 of 78 without them. This association motivates
examining stage structure but does not establish additional predictive
information after adjustment. Sparse and zero-event cells make their
observed rates particularly uncertain. The bins were not optimized as
ecological thresholds, and this cross-tabulation has no fitted interaction
test or cell-specific uncertainty analysis.

### Boundaries of the secondary evidence

The RI comparison is a measurement audit on a smaller, partially overlapping
sample, not a second validation of the main model. On matched microplot
area, the ordinary count equals the sum of RI classes at least one foot
long. The all-length RI total also includes shorter seedlings, so comparing
that total directly with the ordinary count would change the measurement
definition. The observed tall-seedling contrast is not adjusted for ordinary
counts, existing maple stages, sampled coverage, or temporal differences.
Four later-year events cannot support the proposed added-length evaluation
as if it were a well-powered held-out comparison.

The existing survey analysis tests fixed rankings and capacities against
recorded outcomes. It does not measure travel time, treatment response,
independent survey need, or the cost of a wrong decision. No deer-harvest,
browsing, climate, or disturbance dataset has been joined to the core
models. Those external-factor acquisition notes therefore supply neither
an omitted adjusted effect nor additional validation for this paper.
